---
title: "Habit"
---

External habit makes risk aversion move with the surplus of consumption
over a slow-moving habit stock. In good times surplus is high, and
investors are willing to hold risk. In bad times surplus is low, and
marginal utility is high. Investors then demand a large premium to hold
the consumption claim. Moreover, Campbell and Cochrane (1999) use
surplus consumption to match the postwar equity premium at $\gamma = 2$,
and power utility cannot match the same premium at $\gamma = 2$.

Equity is the claim to aggregate consumption, and the bill is the
one-period claim. Consumption growth is i.i.d., and the only state is
log surplus $s_t$. Returns never enter the calibration.

```{python}
import geap

model = geap.CampbellCochraneModel()
res = model.solve()
print(res.compare("equity", "bill").summary())
```

Power utility on a two-state chain, at $\gamma = 2$, produces a premium
well below one point. External habit produces several points and keeps
the bill near 0.94 percent a year (Campbell and Cochrane 1999). The
long-run risks model gets a large premium from persistent consumption
news, rather than from a time-varying surplus.

## Surplus and sensitivity

$$
S_t = \frac{C_t - X_t}{C_t}, \qquad
s_{t+1} = (1-\phi)\bar s + \phi s_t + \lambda(s_t)\,(\Delta c_{t+1}-g).
$$

The sensitivity function $\lambda(s)$ is chosen so the bill is locally
constant ($b = 0$ in Campbell and Cochrane's notation). Steady-state
surplus is $\bar S = \sigma\sqrt{\gamma/(1-\phi)}$.

## Limits

- Habit is external, so the household does not internalise the effect of
  consumption on $X$.
- `CampbellCochraneModel` prices only the consumption claim and the
  bill. A cross-section of dividend claims is not priced yet.
- Unconditional moments come from a simulated monthly path after the
  price-consumption function is solved on a surplus grid. The moments
  move slightly with the grid and the draw.

The source is Campbell and Cochrane (1999), and the bibliography is on
[References](../reference/references.qmd).
